variables.content: For the calculation of adsorption energies and activation barriers for CO oxidation on single-atom catalysts consisting of one transition-metal atom M (M = Fe, Co, Ni, Cu; Ru, Rh, Pd, Ag; Os, Ir, Pt, Au) substituting a surface Fe site on an O3-terminated α-Fe2O3(0001) periodic slab, the Kohn–Sham DFT protocol used here employs the Perdew–Burke–Ernzerhof (PBE) generalized gradient approximation exchange–correlation functional, projector augmented-wave (PAW) pseudopotentials (including mass–velocity and Darwin relativistic corrections but omitting explicit spin–orbit coupling), a plane-wave kinetic-energy cutoff of 400 eV, a 3×3×1 Monkhorst–Pack sampling grid of the surface Brillouin zone, and a DFT+U correction with parameters U = 4 eV and J = 1 eV applied for iron and other strongly correlated 3d metals; the systematic errors of adsorption energies and transition-state barriers arising from this protocol are asserted to be small enough (typical per-barrier uncertainty of order 0.1–0.3 eV) and to lack a consistent bias across the different M values such that the computed ordering (ranking) of the largest cycle barriers (the rate-determining steps) across the twelve metals is reliable for grouping metals into low-barrier versus high-barrier categories under the same modelling conditions.

For carbon monoxide (CO) adsorption on the most favorable close-packed adsorption sites of the group‑VIII 4d/5d metal surfaces Ru(0001), Rh(111), Pd(111), Os(0001), Ir(111), and Pt(111), density functional theory (DFT) total‑energy calculations performed with the Dmol3 code using the revised Perdew–Burke–Ernzerhof generalized‑gradient exchange‑correlation functional (RPBE) and an all‑electron relativistic (AER) core treatment, a uniform (2×2) surface unit cell, a four‑layer slab with the upper two layers relaxed, and the adsorption energy defined as E = E_t − (E_slab + E_CO) yield a set of computed adsorption energies (denoted E1) whose numerical values order the adsorption strengths as Pd > Pt > Rh > Ru > Os > Ir.

The Mason / Abild‑Pedersen linear adsorption‑energy correction $\Delta E = A - B\cdot \nu$ (with the slope parameter $B=0.0008\ \mathrm{eV\cdot cm}$ adopted from the literature and $A$ fitted for the PBE functional) is applied to the computed DFT CO stretching frequencies for the densely packed $(2\sqrt{3}\times2\sqrt{3})R30^\circ$ CO overlayer on Co(0001); under the assumption of transferability of this empirical form to the present compressed overlayer, application of the correction reduces absolute adsorption energies while leaving small relative energy differences and the ordering (A lower than H/F) essentially unchanged.
      Equations (1) and (2) and discussion in Sec. 2 and Sec. 3

The computed per‑metal scalar bonding parameters for the Group‑VIII metals, evaluated in the present calculations and reported here as scaled numerical point values, are (all scalings shown explicitly): $A\times10^{2}$ = Fe 11.47; Co 14.19; Ni 15.99; Ru 2.995; Rh 2.147; Pd 4.153; Os 3.983; Ir 3.321; Pt 5.001. $A_{s}\times10^{2}$ = Fe 11.36; Co 13.92; Ni 15.51; Ru 2.471; Rh 1.575; Pd 4.360; Os 3.307; Ir 2.791; Pt 4.089. $B\times10^{2}$ = Fe 2.895; Co 2.121; Ni 1.539; Ru 13.92; Rh 8.913; Pd 5.935; Os 15.68; Ir 12.19; Pt 9.807. $B_{s}\times10^{2}$ = Fe 2.708; Co 1.976; Ni 1.430; Ru 10.14; Rh 8.307; Pd 5.516; Os 15.10; Ir 11.35; Pt 9.128. The derived single‑site products are $AB\times10^{4}$ = Fe 33.19; Co 30.10; Ni 24.61; Ru 41.69; Rh 19.14; Pd 24.65; Os 62.47; Ir 39.94; Pt 49.05, and $A_{s}B_{s}\times10^{4}$ = Fe 30.75; Co 27.51; Ni 22.18; Ru 25.05; Rh 13.08; Pd 24.05; Os 49.94; Ir 31.69; Pt 37.32. These numerical scalars quantify, on the chosen idealized surface models and within the computational prescription used to obtain overlaps and energy denominators, the relative capacities of the Group‑VIII metals to accept CO lone‑pair density (via $A$, $A_{s}$) and to back‑donate into CO antibonding orbitals (via $B$, $B_{s}$) for end‑on and side‑on contacts.

For CO adsorption on the close‑packed surfaces of the group‑VIII 4d/5d metals Ru, Rh, Pd, Os, Ir, and Pt, the adsorption energy is defined as E = E_t − (E_slab + E_CO), where E_t is the total energy of the relaxed combined slab‑plus‑CO system, E_slab is the total energy of the isolated clean slab (in the same atomic geometry), and E_CO is the total energy of the isolated CO molecule; these energies were computed with the Dmol3 implementation of density functional theory using the revised Perdew–Burke–Ernzerhof generalized‑gradient approximation (RPBE), an all‑electron relativistic (AER) core treatment, a uniform (2×2) surface unit cell, a four‑layer slab with a vacuum region of 12 Å, a 5×5×1 k‑point mesh, relaxation of the upper two slab layers, and convergence tolerances energy 2.0×10^−5 Ha (1 Ha = 27.2114 eV), maximum force 0.004 Ha/Å, and maximum displacement 0.005 Å; the resulting set of computed adsorption energies (denoted E1) for the six metals is on average approximately 5.02% lower than the assembled literature experimental adsorption energies (denoted E5) used as reference in the comparison.
      W. Liu et al., J. Phys. Chem. C (2006) (Table 1)

The linear relation between the computed adsorption energy of acetyl (CH$_3$CO) in a C-bound on-top geometry and the adsorption energy of atomic C was obtained by fitting DFT adsorption energies computed for twelve pure transition-metal surfaces (Re, Ru, Os, Co, Rh, Ir, Ni, Pd, Pt, Cu, Ag, Au) using the authors' DFT protocol (VASP with the PBE functional, PAW potentials, 400 eV cutoff, 7x7x1 Monkhorst-Pack $k$-point mesh, slab models), producing $ \Delta E(\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{CO}) = 0.40\,\Delta E_C + 3.31\ \text{eV}$ with a mean absolute error of $0.10\,$eV; this fit therefore rests on a relatively small sample (N = 12) drawn from pure-element facets and does not include alloys, oxide terminations, alternative facets, or different surface coverage states in the training set.
      Fig. 3

The total energy of an isolated cobalt atom, denoted E_{Co} in the adsorption-energy expression E_ad = -E_{Co/Al} + E_{Al} + E_{Co}, is assumed to have been computed within the same plane-wave density-functional-theory framework (using the same LDA exchange-correlation functional, the same type of ultrasoft pseudopotential for Co, and consistent cell and sampling corrections) so that E_{Co} constitutes a numerically consistent reference energy for adsorption-energy comparisons between different surface sites and does not introduce uncontrolled systematic offsets in the reported adsorption energies.

On the screened series of periodic 2D TM‑PMOF models the most stable adsorption site for a single CO molecule is directly atop the central transition‑metal atom of the porphyrin, forming a TM–C bond, and the computed CO adsorption energies $E_{ads}^{CO}$ (single‑molecule adsorption energies in eV evaluated as total‑energy differences at relaxed geometries in vacuum periodic boundary conditions) are: Ru $-2.66\ \mathrm{eV}$, Os $-2.82\ \mathrm{eV}$ (very strong binding); Fe $-1.42\ \mathrm{eV}$, Co $-1.16\ \mathrm{eV}$, Ir $-1.24\ \mathrm{eV}$, Rh $-1.03\ \mathrm{eV}$ (moderate binding conducive to further hydrogenation); and Ni $-0.05\ \mathrm{eV}$, Pd $-0.05\ \mathrm{eV}$, Cu $-0.12\ \mathrm{eV}$, Pt $-0.13\ \mathrm{eV}$, Zn $-0.20\ \mathrm{eV}$ (very weak binding favoring CO desorption). From these computed adsorption energies the TM‑PMOFs segregate into three operational groups for electrochemical CO$_2$ reduction: (i) very strong CO binders (Ru, Os) that are likely to retain CO as a site‑blocking intermediate (CO poisoning), (ii) moderate CO binders (Fe, Co, Ir, Rh) whose CO adsorption strengths are compatible with further hydrogenation of surface *CO toward deeper reduced products, and (iii) weak CO binders (Ni, Pd, Cu, Pt, Zn) whose CO adsorption strengths favor facile desorption of CO as the dominant product.

The FeO(100) calculations that yield a perpendicular CO molecule bound at a surface Fe top site with a C-Fe bond length of 1.885 Å, an adsorbed C-O bond length of 1.167 Å, and an adsorption energy $E_{ad}=0.81$ eV were performed in CASTEP with ultrasoft pseudopotentials, the generalized gradient approximation in the Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof form, and no on-site $+U$ correction for Fe 3d states. Because omission of $+U$ can change Fe 3d localization, band positions, and adsorption energetics on iron-oxide surfaces, the computed adsorption energy and partial-density-of-states features for CO on FeO(100) can shift under alternative treatments of strong correlation.Fig.3b; Fig.4

We assume the pure-metal reference linear relation
      $BE_{OH}=0.667\cdot BE_O - 8.17\times 10^{-4}\ \text{eV}$,
      where $BE_O$ is the adsorption binding energy (in eV) of an atomic oxygen adsorbate on a pure metal surface and $BE_{OH}$ is the adsorption binding energy (in eV) of a hydroxyl adsorbate on the same pure metal surface, derived from prior DFT binding-energy calculations on twelve pure metals (Fe, Co, Ni, Cu, Ru, Rh, Pd, Ag, Os, Ir, Pt, Au), provides a physically appropriate baseline for measuring perpendicular departures of Pt–M–Pt sandwich catalysts in the $(BE_O,BE_{OH})$ plane across the 28-element Pt–M–Pt dataset.
      [2]

The numeric entries reported in the paper for the change in chemisorption energy per CO molecule—specifically the values −587 eV for Pd‑Co‑Au and −596.52 eV for Pd‑Co‑Ni as printed in the paper's results—are assumed to be correctly reported as physical adsorption energies per CO in units of electronvolts and not to contain typographical errors (for example, missing decimal points), omitted normalization by the number of adsorbates in the supercell, or other unit‑scaling mistakes that would change their order‑of‑magnitude interpretation.

All total-energy and structural-relaxation calculations used spin-polarized Kohn–Sham density functional theory with the Perdew–Burke–Ernzerhof generalized-gradient-approximation exchange–correlation functional (PBE-GGA), the projector-augmented wave (PAW) method for core-valence partitioning, and a plane-wave kinetic-energy cutoff of $470\ \mathrm{eV}$; within this computational setup the relative formation energies between the considered late transition-metal cadmium-substitutional dopants (Fe, Co, Ni, Cu, Ru, Rh, Pd, Ag, Os, Ir, Pt, Au) are treated as sufficiently accurate to establish a thermodynamic stability ranking at the modeled $2.7\%$ concentration without inclusion of beyond-GGA corrections (such as DFT+$U$, hybrid functionals, or many-body perturbation methods) or additional empirical energy corrections.

In the present set of spin-polarized DFT-GGA calculations for transition-metal impurities Cr, Mn, Fe, Co, Ni, Mo, Ru, W, Re and Os substituting Ti in rutile TiO2 at the 12.5% concentration model (Ti14M1M2O32) no explicit on-site Hubbard U correction (DFT+U) was applied to the transition-metal d orbitals; within the scope of the reported results the omission of an explicit U term is taken to indicate that the qualitative oxidation-state assignments from integrated projected d occupancies, the computed local magnetic moments, the signs of impurity–impurity exchange inferred from energy comparisons of collinear initializations and the presence or absence of apparent half-metallic features in the calculated spin-resolved DOS are those produced by plain spin-polarized GGA calculations without on-site U.

The interaction-parameter fits ($V_{\mathrm{gas}},V_{\mathrm{metal}}$) are based on adsorption energies computed with periodic DFT using the PBE exchange–correlation functional, with a plane-wave cutoff energy of $450\ \mathrm{eV}$, four-layer surface slabs (with the two bottom layers fixed to bulk positions), at least $10\ \mathrm{\AA}$ of vacuum in the $z$-direction, convergence criteria of forces below $0.01\ \mathrm{eV/\AA}$ and electronic energy differences below $10^{-7}\ \mathrm{eV}$, and $k$-point sampling densities as reported in the Supporting Information; to compensate known PBE errors in CO adsorption the computed adsorption energies were corrected a posteriori by the C–O stretch dependent correction
      $$
      \Delta E_{\mathrm{c}}(\omega_{\mathrm{CO}})\ (\mathrm{eV}) = 1.92 - 0.0008\,\omega_{\mathrm{CO}}\ (\mathrm{cm}^{-1}),
      $$
      and the interaction parametrization relies on these corrected adsorption energies and the stated DFT slab settings.
      Refs. 7,8,9 (Abild-Pedersen & Andersson; Feibelman et al.; Patra et al.)

The molecular adsorption energy for a carbon monoxide (CO) molecule on a periodic cobalt surface slab is defined as $E_{\mathrm{ads}} = E_{\mathrm{CO/Co\ slab}} - E_{\mathrm{Co\ slab}} - E_{\mathrm{CO}}$, where $E_{\mathrm{CO/Co\ slab}}$ is the converged Kohn–Sham total energy of the periodic slab model with a chemisorbed CO molecule, $E_{\mathrm{Co\ slab}}$ is the converged Kohn–Sham total energy of the corresponding clean periodic cobalt slab, and $E_{\mathrm{CO}}$ is the converged Kohn–Sham total energy of an isolated gas-phase CO molecule computed in a sufficiently large periodic unit cell.
